cases.title: Who's in Charge Here?
cases.presentation: At a warehouse fire with 14 burned workers, a fire captain and an EMS supervisor both arrive and each starts giving orders to the same ambulance crews. Police set up their own post across the street.
cases.question: What fixes this?
options: C: Unified Command: co-locate fire, EMS, and police commanders at one command post with one set of objectives; EMS crews report only through the Medical Group.
D: Each agency keeps its own command post.
cases.explanation: Multi-jurisdiction incidents use Unified Command. Unity of command for crews is restored by clear EMS supervision within the shared structure.
cases.clinicalPearl: One incident, one command post, one plan.

cases.title: Too Many Radios
cases.presentation: You're Medical Group Supervisor at a train derailment. 12 ambulances, 2 rescue teams, and a bus are all calling you directly.
cases.question: Best ICS move?
options: A: Send half the ambulances away.
B: Request a second Incident Commander.
D: Appoint Triage, Treatment, and Transport Unit Leaders and a Staging Manager; units report to them.
cases.explanation: Span of control exceeded → delegate. Unit leaders each supervise a manageable number; you supervise ~4–5 leaders.
cases.clinicalPearl: When the radio never stops, your org chart is too flat.

cases.title: The Handover
cases.presentation: You've been IC at a 9-patient bus crash for 15 minutes. The EMS duty chief arrives and says 'I've got it.'
cases.question: What must happen?
options: A: Face-to-face briefing: situation, hazards, objectives, resources, org chart; chief accepts; transfer announced to all units; you take a new assignment.
B: Hand over your radio and leave.
C: Nothing — rank transfers command automatically.
cases.explanation: A formal transfer of command keeps continuity and tells everyone who's in charge. The outgoing IC usually stays in the structure (e.g., as Medical Group Supervisor).
